content.heading: 1.7 Linear Independence
content.paragraph: The homogeneous equations in Section 1.5 can be studied from a different perspective by writing them as vector equations. In this way, the focus shifts from the unknown solutions of $A\mathbf{x} = 0$ to the vectors that appear in the vector equations.
For instance, consider the equation
This equation has a trivial solution, of course, where $x_{1} = x_{2} = x_{3} = 0$. As in Section 1.5, the main issue is whether the trivial solution is the only one.

content.paragraph: Equation (2) is called a linear dependence relation among $\mathbf{v}_{1}\text{,}\text{…}\text{,}\mathbf{v}_{p}$ when the weights are not all zero. An indexed set is linearly dependent if and only if it is not linearly independent. For brevity, we may say that $\mathbf{v}_{1}\text{,}\text{…}\text{,}\mathbf{v}_{p}$ are linearly dependent when we mean that $\left\{ {\mathbf{v}_{1},}\text{…},\mathbf{v}_{\mathbf{p}} \right\}$ is a linearly dependent set. We use analogous terminology for linearly independent sets.

content.heading: Linear Independence of Matrix Columns
content.paragraph: Suppose that we begin with a matrix $A = \lbrack\mathbf{a}_{1}\mspace{9mu}\cdots\mspace{9mu}\mathbf{a}_{n}\rbrack$ instead of a set of vectors. The matrix equation $Ax = 0$ can be written as
Each linear dependence relation among the columns of $A$ corresponds to a nontrivial solution of $A\mathbf{x} = 0$. Thus we have the following important fact.

note.paragraph: The columns of a matrix $A$ are linearly independent if and only if the equation $A\mathbf{x} = 0$ has only the trivial solution.

content.heading: Sets of One or Two Vectors
content.paragraph: A set containing only one vector—say, $\mathbf{v}$—is linearly independent if and only if $\mathbf{v}$ is not the zero vector. This is because the vector equation $x_{1}\mathbf{v} = 0$ has only the trivial solution when $\mathbf{v} \neq 0$. The zero vector is linearly dependent because $x_{1}0 = 0$ has many nontrivial solutions.
The next example will explain the nature of a linearly dependent set of two vectors.

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Determine if the following sets of vectors are linearly independent.
example.heading: Solution

list.item: Notice that v2 is a multiple of v1, namely v2=2v1. Hence −2v1+v2=0, which shows that {v1, v2} is linearly dependent.

The vectors v1 and v2 are certainly not multiples of one another. Could they be linearly dependent? Suppose c and d satisfycv1+dv2=0If c≠0, then we can solve for v1 in terms of v2, namely v1=(−d/c)v2. This result is impossible because v1 is not a multiple of v2. So c must be zero. Similarly, d must also be zero. Thus {v1, v2} is a linearly independent set.

content.paragraph: The arguments in Example 3 show that you can always decide by inspection when a set of two vectors is linearly dependent. Row operations are unnecessary. Simply check whether at least one of the vectors is a scalar times the other. (The test applies only to sets of two vectors.)

note.paragraph: A set of two vectors $\{\mathbf{v}_{1}\text{,~}\mathbf{v}_{2}\}$ is linearly dependent if at least one of the vectors is a multiple of the other. The set is linearly independent if and only if neither of the vectors is a multiple of the other.

content.paragraph: In geometric terms, two vectors are linearly dependent if and only if they lie on the same line through the origin. Figure 1 shows the vectors from Example 3.

content.heading: Sets of Two or More Vectors
content.paragraph: The proof of the next theorem is similar to the solution of Example 3. Details are given at the end of this section.

note.title: Theorem 7
note.heading: Theorem 7
Characterization of Linearly Dependent Sets
note.paragraph: An indexed set $S = \{\mathbf{v}_{1}\text{,}\text{…}\text{,}\mathbf{v}_{p}\}$ of two or more vectors is linearly dependent if and only if at least one of the vectors in $S$ is a linear combination of the others. In fact, if $S$ is linearly dependent and $\mathbf{v}_{1} \neq 0$, then some $\mathbf{v}_{j}$ (with $j > 1$) is a linear combination of the preceding vectors, $\mathbf{v}_{1}\text{,\,…,\,\,}\mathbf{v}_{j - 1}$.

content.paragraph: Warning: Theorem 7 does not say that every vector in a linearly dependent set is a linear combination of the preceding vectors. A vector in a linearly dependent set may fail to be a linear combination of the other vectors. See Practice Problem 1(c).

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Let $\mathbf{u} = \,\,\begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$ and $\mathbf{v} = \,\,\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 6 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}$. Describe the set spanned by $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$, and explain why a vector $\mathbf{w}$ is in $\text{Span}\{\mathbf{u}\text{,~}\mathbf{v}\}$ if and only if $\{\mathbf{u}\text{,~}\mathbf{v}\text{,~}\mathbf{w}\}$ is linearly dependent.
example.heading: Solution
example.paragraph: The vectors $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ are linearly independent because neither vector is a multiple of the other, and so they span a plane in $\text{ℝ}^{3}$. (See Section 1.3.) In fact, $\text{Span\,\,\{}\mathbf{u}\text{,~}\mathbf{v}\text{\}}$ is the $x_{1}x_{2}\text{-plane}$ (with $x_{3} = 0)$. If $\mathbf{w}$ is a linear combination of $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$, then $\{\mathbf{u}\text{,~}\mathbf{v}\text{,~}\mathbf{w}\}$ is linearly dependent, by transformation (or function or mapping). Conversely, suppose that $\{\mathbf{u}\text{,~}\mathbf{v}\text{,~}\mathbf{w}\}$ is linearly dependent. by Theorem 7, some vector in $\{\mathbf{u}\text{,~}\mathbf{v}\text{,~}\mathbf{w}\}$ is a linear combination of the preceding vectors (since $\mathbf{u} \neq 0)$. That vector must be $\mathbf{w}$, since $\mathbf{v}$ is not a multiple of $\mathbf{u}$. So $\mathbf{w}$ is in $\text{Span\,\,\{}\mathbf{u}\text{,~}\mathbf{v}\text{\}}$. See Figure 2.

image.alt: Two graphs show three linearly dependent and three linearly independent vectors plotted on their respective three-dimensional spaces.

example.paragraph: Click here for an interactive version of Figure 2

content.paragraph: Example 4 generalizes to any set $\{\mathbf{u}\text{,~}\mathbf{v}\text{,~}\mathbf{w}\}$ in $\text{ℝ}^{3}$ with $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ linearly independent. The set $\left\{ \mathbf{u}\textbf{,~}\mathbf{v}\textbf{,~}\mathbf{w} \right\}$ will be linearly dependent if and only if $\mathbf{w}$ is in the plane spanned by $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$.
The next two theorems describe special cases in which the linear dependence of a set is automatic. Moreover, Theorem 8 will be a key result for work in later chapters.

note.title: Theorem 8
note.heading: Theorem 8
note.paragraph: If a set contains more vectors than there are entries in each vector, then the set is linearly dependent. That is, any set $\text{\{}\mathbf{v}_{1},\,\text{…},\,\mspace{-4mu}\mathbf{v}_{p}\text{\}}$ in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$ is linearly dependent if $p > n$.

content.heading: Proof
content.paragraph: Let $A = \lbrack\mathbf{v}_{1}\mspace{14mu}\cdots\mspace{14mu}\mathbf{v}_{p}\rbrack$. Then $A$ is $n \times p$, and the equation $A\mathbf{x} = 0$ corresponds to a system of $n$ equations in $p$ unknowns. If $p > n$, there are more variables than equations, so there must be a free variable. Hence $A\mathbf{x} = 0$ has a nontrivial solution, and the columns of $A$ are linearly dependent. See Figure 3 for a matrix version of this theorem.

note.title: Theorem 9
note.heading: Theorem 9
note.paragraph: If a set $S = \text{\{}\mathbf{v}_{1},\,\text{…},\,\mathbf{v}_{p}\text{\}}$ in $\text{ℝ}^{n}$ contains the zero vector, then the set is linearly dependent.

content.heading: Proof
content.paragraph: By renumbering the vectors, we may suppose $\mathbf{v}_{1} = 0$. Then the equation $1\mathbf{v}_{1} + 0\mathbf{v}_{2} + \cdots + 0\mathbf{v}_{p} = 0$ shows that $S$ is linearly dependent.

Theorem 8 does not apply here because the number of vectors does not exceed the number of entries in each vector. Since the zero vector is in the set, the set is linearly dependent by Theorem 9.

Compare the corresponding entries of the two vectors. The second vector seems to be −3/2 times the first vector. This relation holds for the first three pairs of entries, but fails for the fourth pair. Thus neither of the vectors is a multiple of the other, and hence they are linearly independent.

content.paragraph: In general, you should read a section thoroughly several times to absorb an important concept such as linear independence. The notes in the Study Guide for this section will help you learn to form mental images of key ideas in linear algebra. For instance, the following proof is worth reading carefully because it shows how the definition of linear independence can be used.
